questions.question: What Bible passages support covenant theology?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Gen 17:7, Jer 31:31-34, Heb 8:6-13, Gal 3:29
questions.response:
Covenant theology (or federal theology) understands Scripture as the story of God’s overarching plan of redemption, structured around three foundational covenants: the **Covenant of Redemption** (the eternal pact between the Father and Son), the **Covenant of Works** (with Adam as the representative of humanity), and the **Covenant of Grace** (with Christ as the representative of the elect). Below are the key biblical texts covenant theologians cite, organized by theme.

---

### 1. The Covenant of Redemption (*Pactum Salutis*)
These texts are understood to reveal the eternal agreement within the Trinity to redeem a people for God.

*   **John 6:37–40** – The Father gives a specific people to the Son, and the Son loses none of them but raises them up on the last day.
*   **John 17:1–26** – Jesus speaks of the glory He had with the Father “before the world existed” (v. 5) and of completing the work the Father gave Him to do.
*   **Ephesians 1:3–14** – Describes election “before the foundation of the world” (v. 4) and the predestined plan for adoption through Christ.
*   **Psalm 2** – The Father’s decree to install His Son as King and to give Him the nations as His inheritance.
*   **Philippians 2:5–11** – The Son’s willingness to take the form of a servant in obedience to the Father’s plan.

---

### 2. The Covenant of Works
This refers to the probationary arrangement with Adam, representing all humanity, offering life upon perfect obedience and death upon disobedience.

*   **Genesis 2:16–17** – The command not to eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, with the penalty of death for disobedience. Covenant theologians see this as a “works” principle: “Do this and live.”
*   **Hosea 6:7** – “Like Adam, they have transgressed the covenant” (NASB). Though translation is debated, covenant theologians see this as evidence of a covenant with Adam.
*   **Romans 5:12–21** – Paul explicitly contrasts Adam and Christ as two federal heads. Through Adam’s one trespass, condemnation came to all men; through Christ’s one act of righteousness, justification came to all who believe. This parallel is foundational to federal theology.
*   **1 Corinthians 15:21–22, 45–49** – “For as in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive.” Adam is the “man of dust”; Christ is the “life-giving spirit.”

---

### 3. The Covenant of Grace: Unity and Progression
Covenant theology argues that the Covenant of Grace is one in substance (the promise of salvation in Christ) but administered differently throughout history. These texts emphasize the continuity of God’s people and promises.

#### The Promise Initiated
*   **Genesis 3:15** – The “protoevangelium”: the promise of the seed of the woman who will crush the serpent’s head. Covenant theologians see this as the first announcement of the Covenant of Grace.
*   **Genesis 12:1–3; 15; 17:7** – God’s promise to Abraham includes the promise to be “God to you and to your offspring after you” (17:7). This promise of God as the God of His people is seen as the defining blessing of the Covenant of Grace.
*   **Genesis 26:3–4; 28:13–14** – The Abrahamic promise is reaffirmed to Isaac and Jacob, showing it is an enduring covenant, not merely a temporary ethnic arrangement.

#### The Same Covenant, Different Administrations
*   **Romans 4:1–25** – Abraham was justified by faith, just as New Testament believers are. He is the “father of all who believe” (v. 11), showing that salvation has always been by grace through faith.
*   **Galatians 3:7–9, 15–29** – Those of faith are “sons of Abraham” (v. 7). The promise given to Abraham was not annulled by the Mosaic law (v. 17), and believers are “Abraham’s offspring, heirs according to promise” (v. 29).
*   **Hebrews 11** – The “hall of faith” includes Old Testament saints who were saved by faith in the same promises, looking forward to Christ.
*   **Acts 2:38–39** – Peter declares that the promise is “for you and for your children,” which covenant theologians see as the continuation of the generational promise found in Genesis 17:7.
*   **1 Peter 3:21** – Peter explicitly states that baptism “corresponds to” (or is an antitype of) Noah’s salvation through the flood, linking the New Covenant sign to the administration under Noah.

#### The New Covenant as Fulfillment, Not Replacement
*   **Jeremiah 31:31–34** – God promises a “new covenant” with the house of Israel and Judah. Covenant theologians argue this is the same Covenant of Grace now fully realized in Christ, not a brand-new plan that excludes former believers.
*   **Luke 22:20 / 1 Corinthians 11:25** – Jesus calls the cup “the new covenant in my blood,” showing He is the mediator of the covenant promised in Jeremiah.
*   **Hebrews 8:6–13** – Christ is the mediator of a “better covenant” (v. 6). The author quotes Jeremiah 31 to show that the new covenant makes the old administration “obsolete” (v. 13) in terms of its outward forms (sacrificial system, Levitical priesthood), but not in terms of the underlying substance.
*   **Hebrews 12:22–24** – Believers have come to “Jesus, the mediator of a new covenant,” whose blood speaks a better word than Abel’s.

---

### 4. Federal Headship and Representation
The architecture of covenant theology depends on the biblical concept of representation: Adam represents humanity

questions.question: Where does the Bible teach about the Lord's Supper?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: 1 Cor 11:23-26, Matt 26:26-28, Luke 22:19-20
questions.response:
The Bible teaches about the Lord's Supper (also called Communion or the Eucharist) in several key passages, primarily in the New Testament:

## The Institution of the Supper
The three Synoptic Gospels record Jesus instituting the meal during the Passover with His disciples the night before His crucifixion:

*   **Matthew 26:26–29** – Jesus took bread, blessed and broke it, saying, “Take, eat; this is My body.” Then He took the cup, saying, “This is My blood of the new covenant, which is shed for many for the remission of sins.”
*   **Mark 14:22–25** – A parallel account emphasizing the new covenant and Jesus’ statement that He will not drink of the fruit of the vine again until He drinks it new in the kingdom of God.
*   **Luke 22:14–20** – Includes Jesus’ instruction to **“do this in remembrance of Me,”** and describes the cup as the new covenant in His blood, which is poured out for them.

## Apostolic Teaching on Its Meaning and Practice
The Apostle Paul provides the earliest written account and instructions for the church:

*   **1 Corinthians 11:17–34** – Paul rebukes the Corinthians for their divisive practices, then recounts the tradition he received from the Lord (verses 23–26): Jesus took bread and the cup on the night He was betrayed and said, “This do, as often as you drink it, in remembrance of Me.” Paul concludes that whoever eats the bread or drinks the cup in an unworthy manner is guilty concerning the body and blood of the Lord, and he calls for self-examination.
*   **1 Corinthians 10:14–22** – Paul describes the cup as “the communion of the blood of Christ” and the bread as “the communion of the body of Christ,” warning believers about the seriousness of participation and their unity as one body.

## Early Church Practice
*   **Acts 2:42** – The first believers devoted themselves to the apostles’ teaching, fellowship, the breaking of bread, and prayer. Many scholars understand “the breaking of bread” here as including the regular observance of the Lord’s Supper.
*   **Acts 20:7** – The disciples came together on the first day of the week to break bread, suggesting a regular pattern of observance in the early church.

## Related Teaching
*   **John 6:35–58** – In the “Bread of Life” discourse, Jesus says, “I am the bread of life,” and speaks of eating His flesh and drinking His blood. While Christian traditions differ on how directly this refers to the Lord’s Supper (some see it as primarily referring to faith in Christ’s sacrificial death; others see it as deeply connected to the sacrament), it has historically informed theological reflection on the meaning of Communion.

In summary, the **foundation** for the Lord’s Supper is found in the Gospel accounts of the Last Supper, while its **theological meaning and pastoral practice** are developed most fully in **1 Corinthians 10–11**.

questions.question: What passages address the doctrine of baptism?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Matt 28:19, Acts 2:38-39, Rom 6:3-4, Col 2:11-12
questions.response:
The doctrine of baptism is addressed throughout the New Testament, with key passages touching on its mode, meaning, necessity, and spiritual significance. Here are the major biblical texts organized by theme:

## Institution and Command
- **Matthew 28:19-20** – The Great Commission: "Go therefore and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit."
- **Mark 16:16** – "Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved, but whoever does not believe will be condemned."

## Baptism in the Early Church (Acts)
- **Acts 2:38** – Peter's Pentecost preaching: "Repent and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of your sins, and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit."
- **Acts 8:12-13, 36-38** – Believers (including the Ethiopian eunuch) are baptized upon confessing faith.
- **Acts 10:47-48** – Cornelius and his household are baptized after receiving the Holy Spirit.
- **Acts 16:14-15, 31-33** – Lydia and the Philippian jailer are baptized immediately upon believing.
- **Acts 19:3-5** – Disciples at Ephesus are re-baptized into the name of the Lord Jesus after receiving proper instruction.
- **Acts 22:16** – Ananias tells Paul, "Rise and be baptized and wash away your sins, calling on his name."

## Theological Significance of Baptism (Epistles)
- **Romans 6:3-4** – "Do you not know that all of us who have been baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death? We were buried therefore with him by baptism into death, in order that… we too might walk in newness of life."
- **1 Corinthians 12:13** – "In one Spirit we were all baptized into one body—Jews or Greeks, slaves or free."
- **Galatians 3:27** – "For as many of you as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ."
- **Colossians 2:12** – "Having been buried with him in baptism, in which you were also raised with him through faith."
- **Ephesians 4:5** – "One Lord, one faith, one baptism."
- **Titus 3:5** – God "saved us… by the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit."

## Baptism and Salvation
- **1 Peter 3:21** – "Baptism, which corresponds to this, now saves you, not as a removal of dirt from the body but as an appeal to God for a good conscience, through the resurrection of Jesus Christ."
- **John 3:5** – Jesus says, "Unless one is born of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God" (traditionally interpreted by many, though not all, as referring to baptism).

## Jesus' Baptism and Example
- **Matthew 3:13-17**; **Mark 1:9-11**; **Luke 3:21-22**; **John 1:32-34** – Jesus' own baptism by John, the Spirit's descent, and the Father's declaration.

## Baptism as Ordinance vs. Sacrament
- **1 Corinthians 1:13-17** – Paul downplays personal baptism by his own hands to emphasize the preached gospel, stating, "Christ did not send me to baptize but to preach the gospel."

## Other Notable References
- **Hebrews 6:2** – "Instruction about washings [baptisms]" listed as elementary doctrine.
- **Hebrews 10:22** – "Let us draw near… having our hearts sprinkled clean…and our bodies washed with pure water."
- **1 Corinthians 15:29** – Reference to baptism "on behalf of the dead" (a difficult text with varied interpretations).

---

**Note:** Different Christian traditions organize and interpret these passages differently—whether as a sacrament effecting regeneration (Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran), an ordinance of obedient witness (Baptist, many evangelical), or a covenant sign (Reformed/Presbyterian). The passages above form the common scriptural foundation for all major baptismal theologies.

questions.question: Where does Scripture teach about church government and eldership?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: 1 Tim 3:1-7, Titus 1:5-9, Acts 14:23, 1 Pet 5:1-4
questions.response:
Scripture teaches about church government and eldership in both narrative example and direct instruction, primarily in the New Testament letters to churches and church leaders. Here are the key biblical texts and themes:

## 1. The Office of Elder/Overseer/Shepherd

The New Testament uses three terms interchangeably for the same office:

- **Elder** (*presbyteros*): Acts 14:23; 20:17; Titus 1:5; James 5:14; 1 Peter 5:1
- **Overseer** (*episkopos*, often translated "bishop"): Acts 20:28; Philippians 1:1; 1 Timothy 3:1; Titus 1:7
- **Pastor/Shepherd** (*poimēn*): Ephesians 4:11; Acts 20:28; 1 Peter 5:2

**Key evidence they are the same office:**
- **Acts 20:17, 28**: Paul summons the **elders** (*presbyteroi*) of the Ephesian church and tells them the Holy Spirit has made them **overseers** (*episkopoi*), to **shepherd** (*poimainein*) the church.
- **Titus 1:5-7**: Paul tells Titus to appoint **elders** (v. 5), then immediately says an **overseer** (*episkopos*) must be above reproach (v. 7), using the singular to describe the same role.
- **1 Peter 5:1-2**: Peter exhorts the **elders** to **shepherd** the flock of God, exercising **oversight** (*episkopeō*).

## 2. Plurality of Elders

The consistent New Testament pattern is a plurality of elders in each local church, not a single pastor:

- **Acts 14:23**: Paul and Barnabas "appointed **elders** [plural] for them in **every church** [singular]."
- **Acts 20:17**: Paul called to him the **elders** [plural] of the **church** [singular] at Ephesus.
- **Philippians 1:1**: Paul addresses "all the saints in Christ Jesus... with the **overseers** [plural] and **deacons** [plural]."
- **James 5:14**: "Is anyone among you sick? Let him call for the **elders** [plural] of the **church** [singular]."

## 3. Qualifications for Elders

Scripture gives detailed moral, spiritual, and domestic qualifications:

- **1 Timothy 3:1-7**: Overseer must be above reproach, a one-woman man, sober-minded, self-controlled, respectable, hospitable, able to teach, not a drunkard, not violent but gentle, not quarrelsome, not a lover of money, managing his household well, not a recent convert, well thought of by outsiders.
- **Titus 1:5-9**: Similar list, adding that he must hold firm to the trustworthy word as taught, so that he may be able to give instruction in sound doctrine and also to rebuke those who contradict it.

## 4. Functions of Elders

- **Teaching and Doctrine**: "Let the **elders** who rule well be considered worthy of double honor, **especially those who labor in preaching and teaching**" (1 Timothy 5:17). They must be "able to teach" (1 Timothy 3:2) and hold firm to sound doctrine (Titus 1:9).
- **Ruling/Governing**: Elders are those who "rule well" (1 Timothy 5:17; cf. 1 Timothy 3:4-5). Hebrews 13:7, 17 and 1 Thessalonians 5:12-13 speak of leaders who are "over" the congregation in the Lord and who will give an account.
- **Shepherding/Spiritual Care**: They are to shepherd the flock willingly and eagerly, being examples to the church (1 Peter 5:2-3; Acts 20:28).
- **Prayer**: The elders of the church are called to pray over the sick (James 5:14).

## 5. Distinction Between Elders and Deacons

Elders/overseers are distinct from deacons (Philippians 1:1; 1 Timothy 3:8-13). Deacons are given to "serve" (the Greek *diakoneō* means to serve/minister), but they are not required to be "able to teach" or to exercise the same doctrinal oversight. This creates a two-office structure in the New Testament: elders (who teach and govern) and deacons (who serve).

## 6. Congregational Elements

While elders lead, Scripture also shows the congregation participating in certain decisions:
- **Matthew 18:17**: The final step of church discipline involves telling it to the *church*.
- **Acts 6:3-5**: The apostles had the congregation choose the first deacons.
- **2 Corinthians 2:6**: The majority of the church imposed a punishment.
- **Galatians 1:8-9; 2 John 10**: The congregation is responsible for testing teachers and withholding fellowship from false teachers.

## Summary

The New Testament presents a church government structure in which each local church is led by a **plurality of godly men called elders** (also called overseers or pastors

questions.question: What Bible passages teach about the second coming of Christ?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Acts 1:11, 1 Thess 4:16-17, Matt 24:30, Rev 1:7
questions.response:
The Bible contains numerous passages about Christ's return, spanning the Old Testament, the Gospels, the Epistles, and Revelation. Here are the major texts organized by category:

## The Gospels: Jesus' Teaching
- **Matthew 24–25** (The Olivet Discourse): Jesus describes the signs of the end times, the coming of the Son of Man "on the clouds of heaven with power and great glory" (24:30), and the separation of the sheep and goats (25:31–46).
- **Mark 13:24–27** and **Luke 21:25–28**: Parallel passages to Matthew 24, emphasizing the cosmic disturbances preceding His coming.
- **John 14:1–3**: Jesus promises, "I will come back and take you to be with me that you also may be where I am."
- **Matthew 16:27**: "For the Son of Man is going to come in his Father’s glory with his angels, and then he will reward each person according to what they have done."

## Acts
- **Acts 1:11**: The angels declare to the disciples at the Ascension: "This same Jesus, who has been taken from you into heaven, will come back in the same way you have seen him go into heaven."

## The Epistles
- **1 Thessalonians 4:13–18**: One of the most detailed passages, describing the Lord descending from heaven, the trumpet call of God, the resurrection of the dead in Christ, and believers being "caught up together with them in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air."
- **2 Thessalonians 1:7–10**: Teaches that Jesus will be revealed from heaven in blazing fire with his powerful angels to punish those who do not know God.
- **2 Thessalonians 2:1–8**: Discusses the "day of the Lord," the rebellion, and the revelation of the man of lawlessness, whom the Lord Jesus will overthrow with the breath of his mouth.
- **1 Corinthians 15:51–52**: "We will all be changed—in a flash, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet. For the trumpet will sound, the dead will be raised imperishable, and we will be changed."
- **Titus 2:13**: Encourages believers to live in expectation of "the blessed hope—the appearing of the glory of our great God and Savior, Jesus Christ."
- **Hebrews 9:28**: "So Christ was sacrificed once to take away the sins of many; and he will appear a second time, not to bear sin, but to bring salvation to those who are waiting for him."
- **2 Peter 3:3–13**: Addresses scoffers who question Christ's return, reminding readers that "the day of the Lord will come like a thief" and promising new heavens and a new earth.
- **James 5:7–9**: Exhorts believers to be patient "until the Lord’s coming," comparing it to a farmer waiting for the land to yield its valuable crop.
- **1 John 2:28–3:3**: Encourages believers to continue in Christ so that when He appears, they may be confident and unashamed.

## Revelation
- **Revelation 1:7**: "Look, he is coming with the clouds, and every eye will see him, even those who pierced him."
- **Revelation 19:11–16**: The vision of Christ returning as a victorious warrior-king on a white horse, called "Faithful and True," with a robe dipped in blood and the name "King of kings and Lord of lords."
- **Revelation 22:12–20**: Jesus declares, "Look, I am coming soon! My reward is with me, and I will give to each person according to what they have done... Yes, I am coming soon." The book closes with the Church's prayer: "Amen. Come, Lord Jesus."

## Old Testament Prophecies
- **Daniel 7:13–14**: The vision of "one like a son of man, coming with the clouds of heaven," who is given authority, glory, and sovereign power over all nations.
- **Zechariah 14:4–5**: Prophesies that the Lord's feet will stand on the Mount of Olives, which will split in two, and "the Lord my God will come, and all the holy ones with him."
- **Zechariah 12:10**: "They will look on me, the one they have pierced, and they will mourn for him as one mourns for an only child."

## Common Themes
Across these passages, several consistent themes emerge:
- **Suddenness and certainty**: It will happen unexpectedly ("like a thief in the night").
- **Visibility**: "Every eye will see him"—a public, not secret, event.
- **Resurrection and transformation**: The dead in Christ will rise; living believers will be changed.
- **Judgment and reward**: Christ will judge humanity and establish His kingdom fully.
- **Hope**: His return is the "blessed hope" that motivates holy living and perseverance.

Different Christian traditions (premillennial, amillennial, postmillennial) interpret the sequence and nature of these events differently, but all affirm that Christ will personally, bodily, and gloriously return as promised.

questions.question: Where does the Bible teach about the final judgment?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Matt 25:31-46, Rev 20:11-15, 2 Cor 5:10, Acts 17:31
questions.response:
The Bible teaches about the final judgment in many passages across both the Old and New Testaments. Here are the key texts:

## Old Testament
- **Daniel 12:1–2** – “Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt.” This is one of the clearest Old Testament prophecies of a future resurrection and judgment.
- **Ecclesiastes 12:14** – “God will bring every deed into judgment, with every secret thing, whether good or evil.”
- **Psalm 96:13** / **Psalm 98:9** – The Lord is coming to judge the earth; He will judge the world with righteousness and the peoples with equity.

## The Gospels and Acts
- **Matthew 25:31–46** – Jesus describes the “Son of Man coming in his glory” to separate the nations “as a shepherd separates the sheep from the goats,” judging them according to their deeds.
- **John 5:28–29** – Jesus says, “An hour is coming when all who are in the tombs will hear his voice and come out, those who have done good to the resurrection of life, and those who have done evil to the resurrection of judgment.”
- **Acts 17:31** – Paul declares that God “has fixed a day on which he will judge the world in righteousness by a man whom he has appointed; and of this he has given assurance to all by raising him from the dead.”

## The Epistles
- **Romans 2:5–16** – Paul warns of “the day of wrath when God’s righteous judgment will be revealed,” stating that God “will render to each one according to his works.”
- **2 Corinthians 5:10** – “We must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each one may receive what is due for what he has done in the body, whether good or evil.”
- **Hebrews 9:27** – “It is appointed for man to die once, and after that comes judgment.”
- **2 Timothy 4:1** – Paul charges Timothy “in the presence of God and of Christ Jesus, who is to judge the living and the dead.”

## Revelation
- **Revelation 20:11–15** – This is the most detailed vision of the final judgment: the “great white throne” before which the dead stand. Books are opened, including the book of life, and “if anyone’s name was not found written in the book of life, he was thrown into the lake of fire.”

## Summary
Scripture presents the final judgment as:
- **Certain** – it is an appointed day (Acts 17:31).
- **Universal** – all people, living and dead, will face it (Rev. 20:12; 2 Cor. 5:10).
- **Conducted by Christ** – the Father has given all judgment to the Son (John 5:22, 27).
- **According to deeds** – though the Bible also emphasizes that salvation is by grace through faith, works are the evidence brought to light in judgment (Rom. 2:6; Rev. 20:12).
- **Resulting in eternal destinies** – either everlasting life or everlasting punishment (Matt. 25:46; Rev. 20:15).

While Christians may differ on the exact timing and structure of end-time events (for example, how Revelation 20 relates to Christ’s return), the reality of a final, decisive judgment is a consistent teaching throughout the Bible.

questions.question: What Scripture passages teach about heaven and hell?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Rev 21:1-4, Matt 25:46, 2 Thess 1:9, John 14:2-3
questions.response:
The Bible contains numerous passages describing both heaven and hell. Here are key Scriptures organized by topic:

## **Heaven**

**The Presence of God**
- **John 14:2–3** – Jesus says, “In my Father’s house are many rooms... I am going there to prepare a place for you.”
- **2 Corinthians 5:8** – “We are confident, I say, and would prefer to be away from the body and at home with the Lord.”
- **Revelation 7:16–17** – God will shelter his people; “Never again will they hunger; never again will they thirst... He will wipe every tear from their eyes.”

**The New Creation**
- **Revelation 21:1–4** – “Then I saw ‘a new heaven and a new earth’... There will be no more death or mourning or crying or pain.”
- **Revelation 22:3–5** – “No longer will there be any curse... They will reign for ever and ever.”

**Hope and Citizenship**
- **Philippians 3:20** – “But our citizenship is in heaven. And we eagerly await a Savior from there, the Lord Jesus Christ.”
- **1 Thessalonians 4:16–17** – Believers will be “caught up together... in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air.”
- **Luke 23:43** – Jesus to the thief: “Truly I tell you, today you will be with me in paradise.”

**Rewards**
- **Matthew 5:12** – “Rejoice and be glad, because great is your reward in heaven.”

---

## **Hell**

**Eternal Separation and Punishment**
- **Matthew 25:41** – Jesus describes “the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels.”
- **Matthew 25:46** – “Then they will go away to eternal punishment, but the righteous to eternal life.”
- **2 Thessalonians 1:9** – “They will be punished with everlasting destruction and shut out from the presence of the Lord.”

**Descriptions of Judgment**
- **Mark 9:43–48** – “It is better for you to enter life maimed than with two hands to go into hell, where the fire never goes out... where ‘the worms that eat them do not die, and the fire is not quenched.’”
- **Matthew 13:41–42** – The Son of Man will send out his angels to “weed out of his kingdom everything that causes sin... They will throw them into the blazing furnace, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.”

**The Lake of Fire**
- **Revelation 20:10, 14–15** – “The devil... was thrown into the lake of burning sulfur... Then death and Hades were thrown into the lake of fire. The lake of fire is the second death. Anyone whose name was not found written in the book of life was thrown into the lake of fire.”
- **Jude 1:7** – Sodom and Gomorrah “serve as an example of those who suffer the punishment of eternal fire.”

**Imprisonment**
- **2 Peter 2:4** – God sent angels to “hell, putting them in chains of darkness to be held for judgment.”
- **Luke 16:19–31** – The story of the rich man and Lazarus depicts torment, a great chasm fixed, and agony in flames (often understood as Hades/Sheol prior to final judgment).

---

**Note:** Christian traditions vary in how they interpret some details (for example, whether descriptions of fire are literal or metaphorical, or whether hell involves eternal conscious torment or annihilation). However, these passages form the core biblical teaching that heaven is eternal fellowship with God, while hell is eternal separation from him under divine judgment.

questions.question: Where does the Bible teach the doctrine of creation?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Gen 1:1, John 1:3, Col 1:16, Heb 11:3
questions.response:
The Bible teaches the doctrine of creation most extensively in **Genesis 1–2**, but it is affirmed and developed throughout both the Old and New Testaments.

## Primary Texts

**Genesis 1–2** contains the foundational narrative. Chapter 1 presents a structured, six-day account of God creating the heavens, earth, light, sky, land, vegetation, sea creatures, birds, land animals, and finally human beings (male and female) in His image. Chapter 2 offers a complementary, more detailed account focusing on the creation of Adam and Eve and their placement in Eden. Together they establish that God is the **sovereign, purposeful Creator** who brings order out of chaos and pronounces His work "very good."

## Old Testament Affirmations

Creation is repeatedly celebrated and confessed elsewhere in the Old Testament:

- **Psalm 104** – A poetic meditation on God’s creative power and provision.
- **Psalm 33:6–9** – "By the word of the Lord the heavens were made."
- **Psalm 148** – All creation is called to praise its Maker.
- **Job 38–41** – God answers Job out of the whirlwind with a majestic description of His work in creation.
- **Isaiah 40:28** – The Lord is the everlasting God, the Creator of the ends of the earth.
- **Isaiah 42:5; 45:12, 18** – God declares Himself the maker of heaven and earth, emphasizing that He formed the earth to be inhabited.
- **Nehemiah 9:6** – "You alone are the Lord. You made the heavens... the earth and all that is on it."
- **Proverbs 8:22–31** – Wisdom personified was present with God before and during creation.

## New Testament Affirmations

The New Testament identifies **Jesus Christ** as the agent through whom all things were created:

- **John 1:1–3** – "All things were made through him, and without him was not any thing made that was made."
- **Colossians 1:16** – "For by him all things were created, in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible."
- **Hebrews 1:2, 10** – The Son is the one "through whom also [God] created the world."
- **Hebrews 11:3** – "By faith we understand that the universe was created by the word of God, so that what is seen was not made out of things that are visible."
- **Revelation 4:11** – The heavenly hosts worship God, saying, "For you created all things, and by your will they existed and were created."

## Core Doctrinal Points

Across these passages, Scripture consistently teaches that:
- God is **distinct from** His creation (He is not part of it).
- He created **freely and purposefully** (not out of necessity or pre-existing matter).
- Creation is **good** and reflects His glory.
- Human beings are uniquely made in **God’s image** (Genesis 1:27) with dignity and purpose.

While Christians differ on how to interpret the literary genre and timeframe of Genesis 1–2 (e.g., the length of the "days"), the Bible’s teaching that **God is the Creator of all that exists** is a unanimous and non-negotiable doctrine throughout Scripture.

questions.question: What passages teach about God's providence?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Matt 10:29-31, Rom 8:28, Eph 1:11, Dan 4:35
questions.response:
The Bible teaches God’s providence—His sovereign guidance, care, and control over all creation and human history—in many passages. Here are key Scriptures organized by theme:

## 1. God’s Sovereign Control Over All Things
- **Isaiah 46:9–10** – *“I am God, and there is no other… declaring the end from the beginning and from ancient times things not yet done, saying, ‘My counsel shall stand, and I will accomplish all my purpose.’”*
- **Colossians 1:17** – *“He is before all things, and in him all things hold together.”*
- **Hebrews 1:3** – The Son *“upholds the universe by the word of his power.”*
- **Proverbs 19:21** – *“Many are the plans in the mind of a man, but it is the purpose of the LORD that will stand.”*
- **Daniel 4:35** – God does according to His will among the inhabitants of heaven and earth, and *“none can stay his hand.”*

## 2. God’s Care and Daily Provision
- **Matthew 6:25–34** – Jesus teaches not to be anxious about food or clothing; God feeds the birds and clothes the lilies, and *“your heavenly Father knows that you need them all. But seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you.”*
- **Psalm 104** – A sweeping hymn of God’s providence in creation, sustaining the earth, providing food for every creature, and regulating the seasons.
- **Philippians 4:19** – *“My God will supply every need of yours according to his riches in glory in Christ Jesus.”*
- **Psalm 37:25** – *“I have been young, and now am old, yet I have not seen the righteous forsaken or his children begging for bread.”*

## 3. God’s Direction of Human Events and Hearts
- **Proverbs 16:9** – *“The heart of man plans his way, but the LORD establishes his steps.”*
- **Proverbs 21:1** – *“The king’s heart is a stream of water in the hand of the LORD; he turns it wherever he will.”*
- **Acts 17:24–28** – Paul declares that God made all nations to inhabit the earth, determining their times and boundaries, so that people *“should seek God… in him we live and move and have our being.”*
- **Romans 13:1** – Governing authorities exist because God has established them.

## 4. God’s Providence in Suffering and Evil
- **Genesis 50:20** – Joseph tells his brothers, *“You meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, to bring it about that many people should be kept alive.”*
- **Romans 8:28** – *“We know that for those who love God all things work together for good, for those who are called according to his purpose.”*
- **Job (especially chapters 38–42)** – Though Job suffers terribly, God reveals that His sovereign wisdom governs the universe, and Job confesses that God can accomplish all things and no purpose of His can be thwarted (Job 42:2).
- **2 Corinthians 4:17** – Present affliction is preparing an eternal weight of glory.

## 5. God’s Providence in “Ordinary” and Hidden Ways
- **The Book of Esther** – God’s name never appears, yet His providence is seen in the “coincidences” of timing (Esther becoming queen, Mordecai discovering the plot, the king’s sleepless night) to save His people.
- **The Book of Ruth** – Ordinary events (famine, migration, gleaning in a field, a kinsman-redeemer) weave together to place Ruth in the lineage of King David and Jesus.
- **Acts 8:26–40** – The Spirit directs Philip to the Ethiopian eunuch at the precise moment he is reading Isaiah, leading to his conversion.

## 6. God’s Personal, Intimate Providence
- **Psalm 139:1–16** – God knows when we sit and rise, discerns our thoughts, is acquainted with all our ways, and *“in your book were written, every one of them, the days that were formed for me.”*
- **Jeremiah 29:11** – *“For I know the plans I have for you, declares the LORD, plans for welfare and not for evil, to give you a future and a hope.”*
- **Matthew 10:29–31** – *“Are not two sparrows sold for a penny? And not one of them will fall to the ground apart from your Father… Fear not, therefore; you are of more value than many sparrows.”*

These passages collectively teach that God is not distant or merely watching history unfold; He is actively upholding, directing, and caring for His creation and His people, working even through hardship to accomplish His good purposes.

questions.question: Where does Scripture teach about the nature and practice of prayer?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Matt 6:9-13, Phil 4:6, 1 Thess 5:17, John 14:13-14
questions.response:
Scripture teaches about prayer throughout the entire canon, from Genesis to Revelation. Rather than limiting the teaching to a single passage, the Bible develops a full theology and practice of prayer across many genres—narrative, poetry, prophecy, epistle, and apocalyptic literature.

Here is an overview of where and what Scripture teaches:

## 1. The Old Testament: Foundations and Models
**The Torah and Historical Books** establish prayer as direct human address to the living God. People pray in crisis (Hagar in Genesis 16; Moses throughout Exodus–Numbers), in thanksgiving (Hannah in 1 Samuel 1–2), and in intercession (Abraham for Sodom, Genesis 18; Moses for Israel, Exodus 32). The Tabernacle and later the Temple are designated as a “house of prayer” (Isaiah 56:7), teaching that prayer is connected to God’s presence and atonement, yet it is not confined to a location (Jonah prays from inside a fish, Jonah 2).

**The Psalms** are the Bible’s own prayer book. They teach that prayer includes:
- **Lament** (Psalm 13, 22, 88)
- **Thanksgiving** (Psalm 30, 34)
- **Praise** (Psalm 95, 100, 150)
- **Confession** (Psalm 32, 51)
- **Intercession** (Psalm 20, 67, 122)

The Psalms demonstrate that prayer can be emotional, raw, communal, and deeply honest before God.

**The Prophets** warn that prayer without righteousness is empty (Isaiah 1:15; Jeremiah 14:10–12; Ezekiel 8:18), while also modeling bold intercession (Isaiah 62:6–7; Jeremiah’s confessions; Amos 7).

## 2. The Gospels: Jesus’ Teaching and Example
Jesus provides the clearest instruction on the *practice* of prayer:

- **The Lord’s Prayer** (Matthew 6:9–13; Luke 11:2–4) gives the pattern: prayer is addressed to the Father, seeks His glory and kingdom, asks for daily provision, confesses sins, asks for protection, and acknowledges His sovereignty.
- **Private versus public prayer** (Matthew 6:6) teaches sincerity over performance.
- **Persistence** (Luke 11:5–13; 18:1–8) shows that earnest, ongoing asking, seeking, and knocking reflect faith in God’s goodness.
- **The necessity of faith and forgiveness** (Mark 11:24–25; Matthew 7:7–11) frames prayer within a relationship of trust and reconciliation.
- **Praying “in Jesus’ name”** (John 14:13–14; 16:23–24) indicates that prayer is offered through His person and authority and will be aligned with His purposes.

Jesus also *models* prayer: rising early to pray (Mark 1:35), praying all night before choosing apostles (Luke 6:12), praying at critical moments (the Transfiguration, Gethsemane), and offering the great **High Priestly Prayer** (John 17), which reveals prayer as intimate communion and intercession.

## 3. The Book of Acts: Prayer in the Early Church
Acts shows prayer as the engine of the church’s life:
- The apostles devote themselves to prayer along with the Word (Acts 2:42; 6:4).
- The church prays when appointing leadership (Acts 1:24; 6:6).
- They pray in persecution (Acts 4:23–31), for healing (Acts 9:40; 28:8), for direction (Acts 13:2–3), and for the release of prisoners (Acts 12:5, 12).
- Cornelius’s prayers ascend as a memorial before God (Acts 10:4), showing that God hears the prayers of those who fear Him.

## 4. The Epistles: Theological Instruction
The letters explain the *nature* of Christian prayer under the new covenant:
- **Pray constantly** (1 Thessalonians 5:17) and **in every circumstance** (Philippians 4:6).
- **Pray for all people**, including rulers (1 Timothy 2:1–4), the sick (James 5:14–16), and enemies.
- **Pray according to God’s will** (1 John 5:14–15) and with thanksgiving.
- **The role of the Holy Spirit**: Because believers do not always know how to pray, the Spirit intercedes with groanings too deep for words (Romans 8:26–27).
- **Prayer is Trinitarian**: We pray to the Father (Ephesians 3:14), through the Son (Hebrews 4:14–16; 10:19–22), and by/in the Holy Spirit (Ephesians 6:18; Jude 20).
- **Prayer is warfare** (Ephesians 6:18).

## 5. The Book of Revelation: Eschatological Worship
Revelation frames prayer within the ultimate reality of heavenly worship. The prayers of the saints are pictured as incense before the throne (Revelation 5:8; 8:3–4), and the climax of history includes the final answer to the cry, “How long?” (Revelation 6:10; 22:20). This teaches that prayer is participation in the worship of the Lamb and will be ultimately vindicated.

## Summary of Biblical Teaching
Across these texts, Scripture teaches that prayer is:
- **Relational**: address to a personal, hearing, and answering God.
- **Comprehensive**: including praise, confession, petition, intercession, and lament.
- **Christocentric**: offered through Jesus’ mediation and in His name.
- **Spirit-empowered**: enabled and shaped by the Holy Spirit.
- **Persistent and faith-filled**: expecting God to act according to His will.
- **Communal and individual**: practiced alone and together.

In short, the whole Bible is a manual on prayer, culminating in the truth that believers have bold access to the Father because of the Son, by the Spirit (Ephesians 2:18).

questions.question: What Bible passages relate to Sabbath observance?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Exod 20:8-11, Isa 58:13-14, Mark 2:27-28, Heb 4:9-10
questions.response:
Here are the major biblical passages relating to Sabbath observance, organized by Testament and theme:

## Old Testament

**Creation and Foundation**
- **Genesis 2:2–3** — God rested on the seventh day after creation, blessed it, and made it holy.
- **Exodus 16:23–30** — God provided manna with a double portion on the sixth day so Israel would not gather food on the Sabbath.

**The Ten Commandments and the Law**
- **Exodus 20:8–11** — The Fourth Commandment: "Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy… the Lord blessed the Sabbath day and made it holy."
- **Deuteronomy 5:12–15** — The commandment repeated with a different rationale: observe the Sabbath because God brought Israel out of Egyptian slavery.
- **Exodus 31:12–17** — The Sabbath is a sign of the covenant between God and Israel "forever"; profaning it carried the death penalty.
- **Exodus 35:2–3** — Instructions against kindling a fire on the Sabbath (context of building the Tabernacle).
- **Leviticus 23:3** — The Sabbath is listed as a "holy convocation," a day of solemn rest.
- **Numbers 15:32–36** — The account of a man executed for gathering sticks on the Sabbath, illustrating the seriousness of the command under the Mosaic covenant.

**Prophets**
- **Isaiah 58:13–14** — A call to turn away from personal pleasure on the Sabbath, to "call the Sabbath a delight" and the Lord's holy day.
- **Ezekiel 20:12–20** — God describes the Sabbath as a sign between Him and Israel to sanctify them.
- **Jeremiah 17:19–27** — Warnings against carrying burdens and doing work on the Sabbath, linked to the security of Jerusalem.

## New Testament

**Jesus and the Sabbath**
- **Mark 2:23–28** (parallels: Matthew 12:1–8; Luke 6:1–5) — Jesus declares, "The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath. So the Son of Man is lord even of the Sabbath."
- **Matthew 12:9–14** (parallels: Mark 3:1–6; Luke 6:6–11) — Jesus heals a man with a withered hand in the synagogue, asking whether it is lawful to do good on the Sabbath.
- **Luke 13:10–17** — Jesus heals a crippled woman on the Sabbath, challenging the synagogue ruler's objections.
- **Luke 14:1–6** — Jesus heals a man with dropsy on the Sabbath and asks whether one would not pull a son or an ox out of a well on that day.
- **John 5:1–18** — Jesus heals at the Pool of Bethesda on the Sabbath and tells the healed man to take up his bed, prompting Jewish leaders to begin persecuting Him for Sabbath activity.
- **John 9** — Jesus heals a man born blind on the Sabbath, leading to further controversy with the Pharisees.

**The Early Church and Epistles**
- **Colossians 2:16–17** — "Let no one pass judgment on you… in question of… a Sabbath. These are a shadow of the things to come, but the substance belongs to Christ."
- **Romans 14:5–6** — Paul instructs the Roman church not to quarrel over days: "One person esteems one day as better than another, while another esteems all days alike."
- **Hebrews 4:1–11** — The author speaks of a "Sabbath rest" remaining for the people of God, connecting the seventh-day rest with entering God's ultimate rest through faith.
- **Acts 13:42–44; 16:13; 17:2; 18:4** — Luke records Paul and others meeting in synagogues on the Sabbath to reason with Jews and Gentile God-fearers.

## Note on Interpretation
Different Christian traditions emphasize different passages: Seventh-day Sabbath-keepers typically emphasize the creation ordinance and the Fourth Commandment as perpetual, while many other traditions point to the Colossians and Romans passages to argue that the Sabbath was a shadow fulfilled in Christ, with believers entering a spiritual Sabbath rest (Hebrews 4).

questions.question: Where are the Ten Commandments given in Scripture?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Exod 20:1-17, Deut 5:6-21
questions.response:
The Ten Commandments (or Decalogue) are recorded in two primary places in Scripture:

1. **Exodus 20:1–17** – Given by God at Mount Sinai (Horeb) after the Exodus from Egypt, spoken directly to the Israelites from the mountain.
2. **Deuteronomy 5:4–21** – Restated by Moses to the new generation of Israelites forty years later, just before they entered the Promised Land.

They are also explicitly referred to as the “Ten Commandments” (literally “ten words”) in **Exodus 34:28**, **Deuteronomy 4:13**, and **Deuteronomy 10:4**.

questions.question: Where does Jesus teach the Lord's Prayer?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Matt 6:9-13, Luke 11:2-4
questions.response:
Jesus teaches the Lord's Prayer in two places in the Gospels:

1. **Matthew 6:9–13** – During the **Sermon on the Mount**, Jesus includes it as part of his teaching on prayer, saying, "This, then, is how you should pray" (Matthew 6:9).

2. **Luke 11:1–4** – On a **different occasion**, one of Jesus' disciples asks him, "Lord, teach us to pray," and Jesus responds with a shorter version of the prayer.

While Matthew's account is embedded in a larger discourse about righteous living, Luke presents it as a specific response to the disciples' request for instruction in prayer.

questions.question: Where does the Bible teach about church discipline?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Matt 18:15-17, 1 Cor 5:1-13, Titus 3:10, 2 Thess 3:14-15
questions.response:
The Bible teaches about church discipline primarily in the New Testament, presenting it as a necessary practice for maintaining purity, protecting the flock, and pursuing the restoration of sinning believers. Here are the key passages and principles:

## The Foundational Text
**Matthew 18:15–20** provides the basic procedure:
- **Step 1:** Go privately to the sinning brother or sister and show them their fault (v. 15).
- **Step 2:** If they refuse to listen, take one or two witnesses (v. 16).
- **Step 3:** If they still refuse, tell it to the church (v. 17).
- **Step 4:** If they refuse to listen to the church, treat them as an outsider (a Gentile or tax collector) (v. 17).

## Major Passages on Practice

**1 Corinthians 5**  
Paul commands the Corinthian church to remove an unrepentant man living in sexual immorality. The purpose is to protect the church’s witness and purity: “Expel the wicked person from among you” (v. 13). Paul warns that tolerating unrepentant sin corrupts the whole community (vv. 6–7).

**2 Thessalonians 3:6–15**  
Paul instructs the church to withdraw fellowship from believers who are idle and disruptive, refusing to live according to apostolic teaching. The goal is not punishment but shame leading to repentance (v. 14).

**Titus 3:10–11**  
A divisive person is to receive two warnings, and then they are to be rejected, since they are self-condemned.

**1 Timothy 5:19–20**  
Elders who persist in sin are to be rebuked publicly, so that the rest may stand in fear. This shows discipline applies to leaders too.

**Galatians 6:1**  
Those who are spiritual should restore a person caught in sin gently, keeping watch on themselves.

## The Goal: Restoration
Discipline is not merely punitive. **2 Corinthians 2:5–11** and **2 Corinthians 7:8–13** show that once the Corinthian offender repented, the church was to forgive and reaffirm their love for him, so he would not be overwhelmed by sorrow. Similarly, **James 5:19–20** speaks of turning a wanderer from error to save their soul from death.

## Summary of Biblical Purposes
1. **Restoration** of the sinning believer (Gal. 6:1; James 5:19–20)
2. **Protection** of the church from the spread of sin (1 Cor. 5:6–7)
3. **Honor** of Christ and His name (1 Cor. 5:1–2)
4. **Love** for the offender, refusing to let them persist in destructive sin (Rev. 3:19)

In short, Scripture presents church discipline as an act of love—progressive, careful, and always aimed ultimately at repentance and reconciliation.

questions.question: What Scripture passages teach about Christian liberty?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Gal 5:1, 1 Cor 8:9, Rom 14:1-23, 1 Pet 2:16
questions.response:
The Bible teaches that Christian liberty is not the freedom to do whatever one wants, but freedom from sin, condemnation, and human merit in order to live for Christ. Here are the key Scripture passages organized by theme:

## 1. The Foundation: Freedom in Christ

**Galatians 5:1** – *"For freedom Christ has set us free; stand firm therefore, and do not submit again to a yoke of slavery."*  
Christ’s work liberates believers from trying to earn salvation through the law.

**John 8:32, 36** – *"And you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free... So if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed."*  
True liberty is found in knowing Christ and His redemptive work.

**Romans 8:1–2** – *"There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus. For the law of the Spirit of life has set you free in Christ Jesus from the law of sin and death."*  
Believers are freed from the condemning power of the law and the penalty of sin.

## 2. Freedom from Sin, Not Freedom to Sin

**Romans 6:14, 18, 22** – *"For sin will have no dominion over you... and, having been set free from sin, have become slaves of righteousness... But now that you have been set free from sin and have become slaves of God, the fruit you get leads to sanctification and its end, eternal life."*  
Liberty means we are no longer compelled to obey sin; we are transferred to righteousness.

**Galatians 5:13** – *"For you were called to freedom, brothers. Only do not use your freedom as an opportunity for the flesh, but through love serve one another."*  
Christian liberty must never be used as an excuse for immorality or self-indulgence.

**1 Peter 2:16** – *"Live as people who are free, not using your freedom as a cover-up for evil, but living as servants of God."*

## 3. Freedom from the Ceremonial Law and Human Regulations

**Acts 15:10–11** – *"Now, therefore, why are you putting God to the test by placing a yoke on the neck of the disciples that neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear? But we believe that we will be saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, just as they will."*  
The Jerusalem Council rejected imposing Old Covenant ceremonial law on Gentile believers.

**Colossians 2:16–17** – *"Therefore let no one pass judgment on you in questions of food and drink, or with regard to a festival or a new moon or a Sabbath. These are a shadow of the things to come, but the substance belongs to Christ."*  
Believers are not bound by dietary laws or ceremonial observances.

**Galatians 2:4** – *"Yet because of false brothers secretly brought in—who slipped in to spy out our freedom that we have in Christ Jesus, so that they might bring us into slavery..."*  
Paul warns against anyone who tries to add human requirements to the gospel.

## 4. Liberty in Matters of Conscience

**Romans 14:1–23** – Paul instructs stronger believers not to despise the weak, and the weak not to judge the strong over disputable matters like eating meat or observing certain days. Liberty must be exercised with love and for the building up of others.

**1 Corinthians 8:9** – *"But take care that this right of yours does not somehow become a stumbling block to the weak."*  
Even when we have freedom (e.g., to eat food sacrificed to idols), love may require self-restraint.

**1 Corinthians 10:23, 29** – *"All things are lawful, but not all things are helpful... For why should my liberty be determined by someone else's conscience?"*  
Paul acknowledges Christian liberty while teaching that it be used for edification, not selfishness.

## 5. The Spirit and Liberty

**2 Corinthians 3:17** – *"Now the Lord is the Spirit, and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom."*  
The indwelling Holy Spirit produces liberty, not bondage to external rules.

**James 1:25; 2:12** – James calls God’s Word *"the perfect law, of liberty"* and tells believers to *"speak and so act as those who are to be judged under the law of liberty."*  
True freedom operates under the moral law of God, written on the heart by the Spirit.

## 6. Freedom from the Fear of Death

**Hebrews 2:14–15** – *"That through death he might destroy the one who has the power of death, that is, the devil, and deliver all those who through fear of death were subject to lifelong slavery."*  
Christ liberates His people from the terror of death and judgment.

---

**Summary:** Christian liberty is freedom *from* the guilt and power of sin, *from* the ceremonial law, and *from* human traditions as a means of salvation; and it is freedom *for* joyful obedience, love of neighbor, and service to God through the Holy Spirit.

questions.question: Where does the Bible teach about marriage?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Gen 2:24, Eph 5:22-33, Matt 19:4-6, Heb 13:4
questions.response:
The Bible teaches about marriage in numerous places across both the Old and New Testaments. Here are the major locations and themes:

## Old Testament Foundations
- **Genesis 1:27–28 and 2:18–24**: The foundational account of marriage as God's creation—one man and one woman becoming "one flesh," with the intent of companionship and partnership.
- **Exodus 20:14 and Deuteronomy 5:18**: The commandment against adultery, protecting the exclusivity of the marriage covenant.
- **Leviticus 18 and 20**: Laws prohibiting various unlawful sexual relationships, defining the boundaries of marriage.
- **Deuteronomy 24:1–4**: Regulations concerning divorce (which Jesus later comments on).
- **Proverbs** (especially chapters 5, 18:22, and 31): Wisdom about faithfulness, the blessing of a good spouse, and the dangers of adultery.
- **Song of Solomon (Song of Songs)**: An extended poetic celebration of romantic and sexual love within marriage.
- **Malachi 2:13–16**: God's witness against unfaithfulness; marriage described as a covenant.
- **Ecclesiastes 9:9**: Counsel to enjoy life with one's spouse.

## Jesus' Teachings
- **Matthew 5:31–32; 19:3–12** and **Mark 10:2–12**: Jesus reaffirms Genesis 2:24, teaching that God intended marriage to be permanent and defining the limited grounds for divorce.
- **Luke 16:18**: Further warning against divorce and remarriage.
- **John 2:1–11**: Jesus attends a wedding at Cana, implicitly honoring marriage.

## Apostolic Letters (Epistles)
- **1 Corinthians 7**: Paul's extended teaching on marriage, singleness, sexual relations within marriage, and separation.
- **Ephesians 5:22–33**: The most detailed theological treatment—marriage as a picture of Christ's relationship with the church, with instructions for mutual submission, sacrificial love, and respect.
- **Colossians 3:18–19**: Parallel instructions to husbands and wives.
- **1 Peter 3:1–7**: Guidance on honorable conduct within marriage.
- **Hebrews 13:4**: "Marriage should be honored by all, and the marriage bed kept pure."
- **1 Timothy 3:2, 12 and Titus 1:6**: Marriage and family life as qualifications for church leadership.

## Theological Culmination
- **Revelation 19:6–9 and 21:9**: Marriage is used as the ultimate metaphor for the union between Christ and his people—the "Marriage Supper of the Lamb."

In summary, biblical teaching on marriage is not confined to one passage but developed progressively from creation, through the Law and Prophets, the teachings of Jesus, the apostles' letters, and finally to its ultimate spiritual significance in Revelation.

questions.question: What passages address the role of the civil magistrate?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Rom 13:1-7, 1 Pet 2:13-17, Acts 5:29, Dan 2:21
questions.response:
The role of the **civil magistrate** is addressed in several key biblical texts and in dedicated chapters of the major Reformed confessions:

## Biblical Passages
*   **Romans 13:1–7** — The foundational text; magistrates are ordained by God, bear the sword to punish evil and praise good, and are to be submitted to for conscience' sake.
*   **1 Peter 2:13–17** — Commands submission to every human institution, whether to the emperor or to governors, while honoring all and fearing God.
*   **1 Timothy 2:1–2** — Exhorts prayers and thanksgivings for kings and all who are in high positions, that Christians may lead a peaceful life.
*   **Psalm 82** — God judges the rulers ("gods") for their failure to do justice for the weak and needy.
*   **Deuteronomy 17:14–20** — The law for Israel’s kings, requiring them to rule under God’s law and not turn aside from the commandment.
*   **2 Samuel 23:3** — The ideal ruler is one who “rules in the fear of God.”
*   **Proverbs 8:15–16** — By wisdom kings reign, and rulers decree what is just.

## Confessional Passages
*   **Westminster Confession of Faith, Chapter 23** — Titled *“Of the Civil Magistrate,”* it teaches that civil government is ordained by God for his own glory and the public good, and defines the magistrate’s duty to protect the church and punish offenders.
*   **1689 London Baptist Confession, Chapter 24** — Parallel chapter on the civil magistrate.
*   **Belgic Confession, Article 36** — Addresses civil government as God’s ordinance for restraining evil and protecting the good (note: some modern editions have revised this article).
*   **Second Helvetic Confession, Chapter 30** — Extensive treatment of the duties of magistrates and the duty of subjects.
*   **Scots Confession, Chapter 24** — On the civil magistrate and his responsibility to promote justice and godliness.

If you are looking for the exact wording of a specific confession or catechism, let me know which one and I can provide it.

questions.question: Evaluate this statement from a Reformed perspective: "God elects individuals to salvation based on His foreknowledge of their future faith and repentance."
questions.reference_answer: Election is unconditional, not based on foreseen faith Faith is the result of election, not its cause

required_points: Election is unconditional, not based on foreseen faith
Faith is the result of election, not its cause
scoring.rubric: Must reject the Arminian view of conditional election based on foreseen faith. Should affirm unconditional election per Reformed standards.

questions.response:
From a classical Reformed perspective, this statement is **theologically incorrect**. It describes a view known as **conditional election**—the belief that God’s choice of individuals is contingent upon His foresight of their future faith and repentance. Reformed theology, by contrast, affirms **unconditional election**: God elects individuals to salvation based solely on His sovereign good pleasure and grace, not on any foreseen action, merit, or condition in the creature.

Here is the Reformed evaluation of that statement, broken down by its key theological implications:

### 1. The Reformed Doctrine of Unconditional Election
The Reformed confessions explicitly reject the idea that God’s decree of election rests upon foreseen faith. The **Westminster Confession of Faith** (3:5) states that God has chosen His people in Christ *“without any foresight of faith, or good works, or perseverance in either of them, or any other thing in the creature, as conditions, or causes moving Him thereunto.”* Similarly, the **Canons of Dort** (First Main Point, Article 7) teach that election is *“the unchangeable purpose of God, whereby, before the foundation of the world, He hath out of mere grace, according to the sovereign good pleasure of His own will, chosen… a certain number of persons.”*

In Reformed theology, election is an eternal, free act of God’s will. If God chose because He foresaw that certain individuals would believe, then the ultimate cause of salvation would reside in the human will, not in divine grace. This would compromise *sola gratia*.

### 2. The Biblical Meaning of “Foreknowledge”
Proponents of the statement often appeal to passages like Romans 8:29 (“Those whom he foreknew he also predestined”). However, Reformed exegesis understands *prognōsis* (foreknowledge) in the biblical sense—not as mere intellectual awareness of future events, but as a relational term meaning **to know intimately, lovingly, or to set one’s favor upon** (cf. the Hebrew *yādāʿ* in Genesis 4:1; Amos 3:2).

Thus, Romans 8:29 is not saying, “God foresaw who would believe and therefore predestined them.” Rather, it means, “Those whom God fore-loved, He predestined.” Foreknowledge is not the *cause* of election but a description of God’s gracious, distinguishing love toward those He has chosen.

### 3. The Logical Order of Salvation (*Ordo Salutis*)
In Reformed theology, the causal order runs as follows:

**Election → Effectual Calling → Regeneration → Faith → Justification**

Faith is the **fruit** and **evidence** of election, not its **ground**. Ephesians 1:4–5 says God chose us *before the foundation of the world*, not because we would one day believe, but *“according to the good pleasure of his will.”* Ephesians 2:8 adds that even faith itself is a gift of God, not a native human production. If faith is God’s gift to the elect, then God cannot be electing people based on a faith they do not yet possess and could not generate apart from His grace.

### 4. The Implication of Total Inability
The statement also conflicts with the Reformed doctrine of **Total Depravity** (or Total Inability). Because fallen humanity is spiritually dead (Ephesians 2:1), hostile to God (Romans 8:7), and unable to seek Him (Romans 3:11), no one would ever repent and believe unless God first effectually calls and regenerates them (John 6:44; Acts 16:14).

questions.question: Evaluate this statement from a Reformed perspective: "God's saving grace can be ultimately resisted by the free will of man."
questions.reference_answer: Effectual grace cannot be ultimately resisted God's sovereign call always accomplishes its purpose

required_points: Effectual grace cannot be ultimately resisted
God's sovereign call always accomplishes its purpose
scoring.rubric: Must reject the Arminian doctrine of resistible grace. Should affirm irresistible (effectual) grace.

questions.response:
From a Reformed perspective, this statement is **theologically incompatible** with the biblical doctrine of salvation and must be rejected. It contradicts the Reformed understanding of God’s sovereignty in redemption, the depth of human depravity, and the efficacy of divine grace.

Here is the evaluation broken down according to Reformed theology:

## 1. It Denies Irresistible (Efficacious) Grace
The statement directly opposes the Reformed doctrine of **irresistible grace** (better termed *efficacious grace*), the fourth point of the **Canons of Dort** and a central pillar of Reformed soteriology.

Reformed theology teaches that when God purposes to save His elect, He does not merely make salvation *possible* and then wait to see if the human will cooperates. Rather, He **effectually calls** His people by the Holy Spirit. The Canons of Dort state that the regenerating Spirit "penetrates into the inmost being of man, opens the closed heart, softens the hard heart... [and] infuses new qualities into the will, making the dead will alive, the evil one good, the unwilling one willing, and the stubborn one compliant" (III/IV, Art. 11).

Saving grace is not an offer that can be thwarted; it is a divine power that **infallibly accomplishes** its intended purpose. As the Westminster Confession of Faith teaches, God effectually calls the elect, "enlightening their minds... and renewing their wills... [so] they come most freely, being made willing by His grace" (WCF 10.1).

## 2. It Misunderstands the Reformed View of Free Will
Reformed theology does not deny that man has a will or that he makes genuine choices. However, it rejects the notion of **libertarian free will**—the idea that the unregenerate will is neutral or able to choose spiritual good apart from grace.

Because of **Total Depravity**, the unregenerate human will is not free in the sense of being liberated from sin; it is **enslaved to sin** (Romans 6:17, 20; John 8:34). The natural man cannot submit to God's law (Romans 8:7) and will not come to Christ (John 6:44). Therefore, the idea that "free will" can ultimately resist saving grace assumes a capacity in fallen man that Reformed theology denies he possesses.

The Reformed view is **compatibilist**: man acts freely according to his strongest desires, but those desires are bound by a sinful nature until God regenerates the heart.

## 3. It Implies Synergism, Not Monergism
The statement reflects a **synergistic** view of salvation (a cooperation between God and man where man has the final say). Reformed theology is strictly **monergistic**: salvation is the work of God alone from beginning to end. 

God does not do 99% and then wait for the human will to supply the final 1%. Regeneration is not a joint venture. If God's saving grace could be ultimately resisted, then the decisive factor in salvation would not be God's sovereign mercy but the autonomous human will. This robs God of glory and makes the sinner his own savior.

## 4. The Crucial Distinction: Common Grace vs. Saving Grace
Reformed theology does acknowledge that grace can be resisted in one sense. **Common grace**—the general work of the Spirit through the preached Word and the conscience—can be and often is resisted, rejected, and spurned by sinners (Acts 7:51). The **general call** of the gospel goes out to all, and many refuse it.

However, **saving grace** (or **special grace**) is different. God's **effectual call** is His inward, powerful summons to the elect. While the general call can be resisted, the effectual call cannot. Jesus declared, "All that the Father gives me will come to me" (John 6:37) and "No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him" (John 6:44). The drawing of the Father is not a weak invitation but an almighty act that ensures the elect will come.

## 5. Biblical and Confessional Basis
Reformed theology grounds this doctrine in Scripture:
- **John 6:37, 44**: The Father's gift to the Son results in certain coming; the Father's drawing enables coming.
- **Romans 8:29-30**: Those predestined are called, justified, and glorified with no drop-offs in the chain.
- **Ephesians 1:4-5, 11**: Salvation is according to the purpose of God's will, not the will of the flesh.
- **Philippians 2:13**: God works *in* us both to will and to work for His good pleasure.
- **Ezekiel 36:26-27**: God removes the heart of stone and gives a heart of flesh, causing His people to walk in His statutes.

The **Westminster Confession of Faith** (3:6; 9:4; 10:1-2) and the **Canons of Dort** (Heads III/IV) explicitly reject the idea that the human will can frustrate God's decree or resist His effectual purpose to save.

## Conclusion
From a Reformed perspective, the statement "God's saving grace can be ultimately resisted by the free

questions.question: Evaluate this statement from a Reformed perspective: "A truly regenerate believer can fall away from grace and lose their salvation."
questions.reference_answer: True believers cannot lose salvation God preserves the elect

required_points: True believers cannot lose salvation
God preserves the elect
scoring.rubric: Must reject the possibility of losing salvation. Should affirm the perseverance and preservation of the saints.

questions.response:
From a Reformed perspective, this statement is **false**. It directly contradicts the doctrine of the **perseverance of the saints** (more accurately called the **preservation of the saints**), which is a cornerstone of Reformed soteriology classically summarized in the Canons of Dort and the Westminster Confession of Faith.

Here is the evaluation broken down according to Reformed theological principles:

### 1. The Reformed Affirmation: True Believers Persevere to the End
Reformed theology teaches that those whom God has **truly regenerated**—effectually called, justified, and adopted—**cannot finally fall away from grace or lose their salvation**. This is not because of the believer’s own inherent ability to "hold on," but because of God’s sovereign power and faithfulness to preserve His elect.

Key biblical foundations cited include:
*   **John 10:28–29**: No one can snatch Christ’s sheep out of His or the Father’s hand.
*   **Romans 8:30**: Those God predestined, He called; those He called, He justified; those He justified, He glorified. The chain is unbroken; none drop out between justification and glorification.
*   **Philippians 1:6**: He who began a good work in you will bring it to completion.
*   **1 Peter 1:5**: Believers are "kept by the power of God through faith for salvation."
*   **Jude 24**: God is able to keep His people from stumbling and to present them blameless.

### 2. The Nature of Regeneration
In Reformed theology, regeneration is not merely a moral improvement or a human decision; it is a **monergistic work of the Holy Spirit** that raises the spiritually dead to life (Ephesians 2:1–5; John 3:3–8). It involves the implanting of a new, living faith and a new heart with new affections oriented toward God. Because this work originates in God’s unchangeable purpose and is sealed by the indwelling Holy Spirit (Ephesians 1:13–14), it is irreversible. A truly regenerate person has been given a principle of spiritual life that, by God’s preserving grace, will endure.

### 3. Handling the "Warning Passages"
Reformed theologians do not ignore the many biblical warnings against apostasy (e.g., Hebrews 6:4–6; Hebrews 10:26–29; 2 Peter 2:20–22). They interpret these passages in two primary ways:

*   **Hypothetical Warnings**: Some warnings describe the dreadful consequences of apostasy *if* it were possible for the elect, serving as means God uses to keep His people from drifting. The warnings are real, but their effect is to drive believers to cling to Christ, not to suggest that God’s elect will actually fall away.
*   **Describing False or Temporary Professors**: More commonly, Reformed exegesis argues that these passages describe people who had **external, historical contact with the means of grace**—perhaps even experiencing powerful, emotional convictions of sin and temporary moral reform—but who were never truly regenerate. They are like the stony-ground hearers in the Parable of the Sower (Matthew 13:20–21): they spring up quickly but have no root.

**1 John 2:19** is pivotal here: "They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would have continued with us. But they went out, that it might become plain that they all are not of us." From this, Reformed theology concludes that **final apostasy proves that the person was never a true believer**, regardless of how convincing their external profession may have been.

### 4. Falling into Sin vs. Falling Away from Grace
Reformed theology carefully distinguishes between a believer **falling into grievous sin** (backsliding) and **falling away from grace** (final apostasy).

*   A true believer can fall into serious, habitual sin for a season (think of David’s adultery and murder, or Peter’s denial). This brings divine discipline, fatherly chastisement, and grief to the Spirit.
*   However, a true believer **cannot** totally or finally lose the grace of God. The new nature given in regeneration will inevitably produce repentance. God restores His wandering sheep; He does not lose them.

As the Westminster Confession of Faith states: "They whom God hath accepted in His Beloved, effectually called and sanctified by His Spirit, can neither totally nor finally fall away from the state of grace; but shall certainly persevere therein to the end, and be eternally saved" (WCF 17.1).

### 5. The Relationship Between Divine Preservation and Human Perseverance
Reformed theology rejects both **easy-believism** (antinomianism) and the idea that perseverance is a passive, automatic guarantee regardless of one’s life. Instead, it teaches that:
*   God **preserves** His elect through the means of grace: the Word, prayer, the sacraments, and fellowship.
*   Believers **actively persevere** by continuing in faith and repentance. This perseverance is itself a gift of God (Acts 13:43; Colossians 1:21–23), not a meritorious work. The believer "works out [their] salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God who works in you, both to will and to work for his good pleasure" (Philippians 2:12–13).

### 6. Pastoral and Theological Conclusion
The statement that a regenerate believer can lose salvation is, from the Reformed perspective, a denial of God’s omnipotent faithfulness and the efficacy of Christ’s atoning work. If salvation could be lost, it would imply that:
*   The Father’s election could fail.
*   The Son’s atonement and intercession are insufficient to save completely.
*   The Holy Spirit’s sealing and indwelling can be revoked by human will or failure.

Instead, the Reformed faith offers the doctrine of perseverance as a **comfort** to trembling consciences: the security of the believer rests not on their own fickle hold on Christ, but on Christ’s unbreakable hold on them. As Jesus said, "I give them eternal life, and they will never perish" (John 10:28).

questions.question: Evaluate this statement from a Reformed perspective: "Christ died equally for every individual person, intending to save all without distinction."
questions.reference_answer: The atonement is particular and definite Christ died especially for the elect

required_points: The atonement is particular and definite
Christ died especially for the elect
scoring.rubric: Must reject universal atonement in intent. Should affirm particular redemption while acknowledging sufficiency for all.

questions.response:
From a classic, confessional Reformed perspective, this statement is **erroneous**. It reflects a doctrine of universal or general redemption rather than the Reformed doctrine of **particular redemption** (often called “limited atonement,” though Reformed theologians prefer to say the atonement is *limited in intent* but *unlimited in value*).

Here is the evaluation broken down according to Reformed theology:

---

### 1. Particular Intent, Not Equal Universal Intent
Reformed theology confesses that Christ’s death had a **specific, effectual purpose**: to actually secure the salvation of His elect, not merely to make salvation possible for every individual equally.

The **Canons of Dort** (Second Main Point of Doctrine, Articles 8–9) state that Christ’s death was efficacious for the elect and that it was God’s purpose that Christ should “effectually redeem… all those, and those only, who were from eternity chosen to salvation.” Similarly, the **Westminster Confession of Faith** (8.5) teaches that Christ purchased “an everlasting inheritance in the kingdom of heaven, for **all those whom the Father hath given unto Him**.”

If Christ died **equally for every individual person** with the **equal intention** of saving each one, then His atonement does not actually save anyone in and of itself; it only creates a possibility contingent upon human response. This undermines monergistic grace and edges toward the Arminian view that Christ’s death made salvation *possible* but not *certain* for anyone in particular.

### 2. The Crucial Distinction: Sufficiency vs. Efficiency
Reformed theology does teach that the **value** (sufficiency) of Christ’s sacrifice is infinite and sufficient to cover the sins of the whole world. The **Canons of Dort** explicitly affirm this (II.3): Christ’s death is “abundantly sufficient to expiate the sins of the whole world.”

However—and this is the critical distinction—Reformed theology separates **sufficiency** from **efficiency**. Christ’s blood is *sufficient* for all, but it was *intended* to be efficient only for the elect. To say He died “equally” for every individual in *intent* collapses this distinction. As John Owen famously argued, if God intended to save every individual, then either:
1. God **failed** in His intention (since not all are saved), or
2. Salvation depends ultimately on the **will of man** (since the cross only makes it possible, and man must make it actual).

Neither option is acceptable in Reformed theology.

### 3. “All Without Distinction” vs. “All Without Exception”
The statement uses the phrase “all without distinction,” which in some theological contexts means “all kinds of people, without national, ethnic, or social distinction” (cf. Rev. 5:9; Gal. 3:28). Reformed theology gladly affirms this: the elect are gathered from every tribe, tongue, people, and nation.

However, in the statement provided, “all without distinction” is clearly coupled with “every individual person,” meaning **all without exception**. This is incompatible with particular redemption. Christ laid down His life for **His sheep** (John 10:14–15), for **His church** (Acts 20:28; Eph. 5:25), and for those given to Him by the Father (John 6:37–39; 17:9). He prays explicitly *not* for the world in the same way He prays for the elect (John 17:9).

### 4. The Universal Free Offer of the Gospel
The Reformed tradition is **not** hyper-Calvinist. It believes the Gospel is to be preached **indiscriminately** to all people everywhere. God sincerely commands all men everywhere to repent, and the offer of salvation is genuine. However, this universal *offer* does not require a universal *atonement in intent*. The preacher may say, “Christ will save all who believe,” because anyone who comes to Christ in faith will find that He is indeed their Savior. But the reason any person believes is because the Spirit effectually calls those for whom Christ specifically died.

### 5. The Amyraldian Exception (And Its Rejection)
A minority report within Reformed history—**Amyraldism** (or hypothetical universalism)—proposed that God intended Christ’s death for all humanity *hypothetically*, but only the elect actually receive it due to God’s decree of election. Even this view, however, was controversial and rejected by the mainstream Reformed confessions. Furthermore, the Amyraldian position still does not typically affirm that Christ died “equally” for every individual in the same sense as the statement in question. Classic Reformed theology sees even Amyraldism as an unstable compromise.

### Conclusion
The statement “Christ died equally for every individual person, intending to save all without distinction” is **incompatible with confessional Reformed theology**. It denies particular redemption by asserting a universal, undifferentiated salvific intention in God’s eternal decree and in the cross itself.

The Reformed confession is rather that Christ’s atonement is of infinite **worth** for all, but of special, effectual **intent** for the elect alone—purchasing not just an opportunity for salvation, but salvation itself, including faith, repentance, and eternal glory, for all those the Father gave Him.
